\chapter{Tables}\label{ch:tables}
% Four weight tables may stack at the top of a page (main.tex restores the default of 3 after this chapter).
\setcounter{topnumber}{4}

The tables of this chapter are the single source of the weights and constants that Part~I quotes. Every body was
written by the book's data generator from the library itself, from the same internal tables that
\code{derivative} uses (the few constants that are literals of the library's code are transcribed, as
\cref{sec:tables-ridders} says), and the generator checks each rule against its moment conditions before writing it;
the library's tests compare the rules with the published tables of Fornberg\cite{fornberg1988} and
Chapra.\cite[ch.~23]{chapra2015}

\section{How to read the tables}\label{sec:tables-reading}

A rule of accuracy order $\aorder$ for the derivative of order $\dorder$ samples $f$ at the nodes $x + n_k h$ and
combines the samples with integer numerators $c_k$ over one denominator $\den$:
\begin{equation}
  f^{(\dorder)}(x) \approx \frac{1}{\den\, h^{\dorder}} \sum_k c_k\, f(x + n_k h).
  \label{eq:tables-rule}
\end{equation}
The weights of \cref{ch:taylor,ch:stencils} are $w_k = c_k / \den$. They are fixed by the moment conditions
(\cref{sb:moments}): with $\mom{j} = \sum_k c_k n_k^j$,
\begin{equation}
  \mom{\dorder} = \dorder!\, \den, \qquad \mom{j} = 0 \quad \text{for } j \ne \dorder,\ 0 \le j < \dorder + \aorder.
  \label{eq:tables-moments}
\end{equation}
The first moment that does not vanish gives the leading error term: the rule's value minus $f^{(\dorder)}(x)$ is about
$\pm \errc h^{\aorder} f^{(\dorder+\aorder)}(x)$, with the error constant $\errc = \abs{\mom{\dorder+\aorder}} /
((\dorder+\aorder)!\, \den)$ and the sign given in the last column. The amplification $\ampl = \sum_k \abs{c_k} /
\den$ multiplies the rounding of the samples: their rounding error reaches the result as about $\ampl \epsmach
\abs{f} / h^{\dorder}$. Both enter the error model of \cref{ch:stencils}.

The central rules use the $\aorder + \dorder - 1$ integers around 0, without 0 for odd $\dorder$, whose weight would
be zero. The forward rules use $0, 1, \ldots, \aorder + \dorder - 1$. \code{Backward<P>} is \code{Forward<P>}
mirrored: its nodes are those of \code{Forward<P>} negated, and its numerators those of \code{Forward<P>} times
$(-1)^{\dorder}$, with the same $\den$, $\ampl$ and $\errc$; the sign of its leading term changes for odd $\aorder$.
It is not tabulated.

\section{Central rules}\label{sec:tables-central}

\Cref{tab:weights-central-first,tab:weights-central-second,tab:weights-central-third,tab:weights-central-fourth}
give \code{Central<P>} for $\dorder = 1$ to 4 and $\aorder = 2$ to 10. Each pair of nodes adds two orders; $\errc$
falls quickly with $\aorder$ and $\ampl$ grows slowly, which is why the central rules of high order pay off in wide
types (\cref{tab:accuracy-matrix}). The cap at $\aorder = 10$ is a design decision (\code{docs/PHASE2_API.md}): by
the model's exponent alone, a \code{Central<12>} would gain about \num{\valCapGainCentralTwelveFirstDouble} digit for
$f'$ in double and \num{\valCapGainCentralTwelveFirstMultiprecision} in a 50-digit type (for $f''''$,
\num{\valCapGainCentralTwelveFourthDouble} and \num{\valCapGainCentralTwelveFourthMultiprecision}), over a stencil on
which $f$ must be smooth that much wider, and the library stops there. The rules with $\aorder = 2$ are the textbook formulas: the central difference,
the three-point second difference, the four-point rule for $f'''$ and the five-point rule for $f''''$.

\section{Forward rules}\label{sec:tables-forward}

\Cref{tab:weights-forward-first,tab:weights-forward-second,tab:weights-forward-third,tab:weights-forward-fourth}
give \code{Forward<P>} for $\dorder = 1$ to 4 and $\aorder = 1$ to 6. A one-sided rule gains one order per node, and
both its constants are larger than those of the central rule of the same order: $\ampl$ grows to
\num{\valAmplForwardSix} for $f'$ with $\aorder = 6$ and to \num{\valAmplForwardSixFourth} for $f''''$. The cap at
$\aorder = 6$ is a design decision (\code{docs/PHASE2_API.md}): beyond it the amplification grows about as fast as the
higher order pays, by the model, so the library stops there.

\section{Default steps and model accuracy}\label{sec:tables-steps}

\Cref{tab:default-steps} gives, for every stencil and order, the exponent of the default step
$h = \epsmach^{1/(\aorder+\dorder)} \max(\abs{x}, 1)$, the step itself for \code{double} at $\abs{x} \le 1$ (for a
larger $\abs{x}$, multiply by $\abs{x}$), the model's relative error $\epsmach^{\aorder/(\aorder+\dorder)}$ at that
step, and the number of evaluations. The steps are \code{nxx::math::root_epsilon<P + N, double>()}, computed by the
library. The model error drops the constants $\errc$ and $\ampl$ and assumes that $f$ varies on the scale
$\max(\abs{x}, 1)$, $\abs{f} \sim s^{\dorder} \abs{f^{(\dorder)}}$; it is a rule of thumb, and the measured
accuracies are in \cref{tab:accuracy-matrix}.

\section{Ridders' constants}\label{sec:tables-ridders}

\Cref{tab:ridders-constants} collects the constants of Ridders' method, the same for every derivative order except
where the value depends on $\dorder$; \cref{ch:ridders} and \cref{sb:floor-coverage} explain them, and the design
record in the repository (\code{docs/PHASE3_API.md}, \code{docs/PHASE4_API.md}) gives the evidence for each choice.
The level cap and the initial-step divisors are read from the library; the ratio, the stall and the two factors of
the untrusted-result test are literals of its code, transcribed by the generator.

The level cap counts every level attempted, restarts included; with two or four evaluations per level it gives the
maximum evaluations of the last row.
